paragraphs: Museum technicians and conservators (O*NET-SOC 25-4013.00) assess whether museum objects need conservation, select the safest and most effective treatments, perform cleaning, consolidation, infilling, and documentation, and install and arrange objects for exhibitions. Their work creates reviewable records of object condition, treatment rationale, and results while avoiding further damage.

If you willingly test and consult documentation before treatment, accept repeated consideration of minimal intervention, distinguishability, and reversibility, and remain patient with material, technique, and historical details, these are more useful positive signals than simply liking cultural objects.

Caution signals include handling objects without testing and approval, using irreversible materials or obscuring original information, or assigning high-risk treatment to unqualified people with incomplete records. These problems can cause irreversible losses and affect collection and research value.

Start with a paper condition report exercise: Using an entirely fictional object file with material, date, deterioration descriptions, and photo captions, describe tests, candidate treatments and a no-treatment option, risk and reversibility assessments, approvals, and record fields. Identify three safety and ethical confirmation points. Use only fictional or public examples and do not handle real collections.

Museum Technicians and Conservators correspond to O*NET-SOC 25-4013.00 (the page is labeled Bright Outlook). The official definition is to restore, maintain, or prepare objects in museum collections for storage, research, or exhibition. They may work with fossils, skeletal parts, or botanical specimens, or with artifacts, textiles, or art; may identify and record objects or install and arrange exhibits; and include book and document conservators.

Work usually starts with condition assessment: Check collection files and research, assess the nature and causes of deterioration, perform standard chemical and physical tests when needed, and decide whether to treat and which method is safest and most effective. Retain photographs, test data, and written records before and after treatment.

entries: Condition assessment and treatment selection: Determine whether objects need conservation, select the safest and most effective methods, and assess treatment and no-treatment risks.
Material-specific treatment: Perform cleaning, consolidation, and infilling in specialties such as documents and books, paintings, decorative arts, textiles, metals, or architectural materials.
Testing and preservation advice: Perform standard chemical and physical tests and advise curatorial and architectural staff on preservation procedures such as temperature and humidity control.
Restoration and infilling: Repair, restore, and reassemble objects, design and make missing or damaged parts, and prevent further deterioration.
Documentation and collection management: Photograph and register objects, enter collection information into databases, and maintain treatment reports and work records.
Exhibitions and collaboration: Install, arrange, and prepare exhibits while ensuring object safety; coordinate outside experts, volunteers, and students; and provide public education when needed.

paragraphs: Work context (O*NET survey): 96% consider accuracy extremely important; 88% use email daily; 76% work in controlled indoor environments daily and 76% use their hands to handle or feel objects almost continually; 60% have face-to-face discussions daily; 38% rate error consequences as extremely serious; 38% consider competition extremely intense and 42% very intense; and 80% work 40 hours weekly.

Preparation and training: O*NET places this occupation in Job Zone 5 (SVP 8.0 and above, requiring extensive professional preparation), with most requiring graduate degrees. The O*NET national training directory lists 500 programs in areas such as art history and conservation and museum studies. BLS notes that archivists, curators, and conservators typically need a related master's degree, while museum technicians typically need a bachelor's degree. Internship or volunteer experience is helpful.

Key professional judgments: Distinguish deterioration caused by material aging, environmental fluctuations, past treatment residues, or accidental damage; assess treatment reversibility and distinguishability; and decide when outside experts or interdisciplinary consultation are needed. Leading O*NET work activities are documenting information (94), handling and moving objects (93), making decisions and solving problems (93), identifying objects, actions, and events (89), and obtaining information (88).

Main outputs are condition and treatment records: Test reports, treatment plans and approval records, before-and-after photographs, materials and formulations used, collection database entries and registration numbers, and exhibition installation and safety records. Environmental and follow-up monitoring recommendations are still needed after treatment.

Work cycle: Object retrieval and file checks, condition testing and deterioration records, treatment planning and risk approval, cleaning, consolidation and infilling, treatment records and database updates, environmental and preservation advice, and exhibition installation and handover. Every step is traceable and reviewable.

Archivists and curators manage collecting systems, research, and exhibition content, taking responsibility for objects' meaning, provenance, and display interpretation. Museum technicians and conservators assess and treat specific objects. Choosing collection and exhibition content differs from hands-on control of an object's deterioration and maintaining records.

These comparisons draw on the O*NET O*NET-SOC 25-4013.00 definition, tasks, and adjacent occupation list, and BLS definitions relayed by O*NET. Comparison dimensions are editorial syntheses, not official rankings or hiring standards.

First distinguish responsibility for collection and exhibition content from responsibility for specific object conditions and treatments. Then compare adjacent directions' objects, decision authority, and ethical boundaries rather than institution types alone.

Curators handle collection research, interpretation, and exhibition content; archivists handle arrangement, cataloging, and long-term accessibility of records. Museum technicians and conservators handle object condition assessment, treatment, and documentation, with treatment plans generally requiring curatorial or conservation lead approval.

If you prefer research, interpretation, and exhibition content planning, compare curators or archivists first. If you prefer hands-on condition assessment, testing, treatment, and technical records, this occupation is more direct.
Entry-level staff and assistants

First master condition documentation, testing, and materials knowledge, then treat low-risk objects under supervision. Digital and imaging tools can reduce documentation burdens but do not replace treatment judgments.
Independent conservators
Treat digital images, spectra, and test data as part of the evidence. People still assess reversibility and distinguishability, select materials, and sign treatment plans.
Collection management and registration roles
Use collection databases and search tools to improve cataloging and traceability while checking consistency among provenance, numbers, and images, retaining human review.
External communication and education roles
Use digital exhibitions and online resources to expand public education, but professionally review information on physical conditions, treatment details, and collection security before publication.

Editorial trial-use suggestion: Apply AI to cataloging, searches, image previews, and report drafts, measuring errors, review effort, and hours. Actual occupational adoption and efficiency evidence was not obtained. Condition judgments, material selection, physical treatment, and authorization remain subject to professional review; generated suggestions must not independently determine treatment. Verifiable reference: In 2025, average annual wages in culture, sports, and entertainment were 129,447 yuan/year in urban non-private units (nominal growth of 2.7%) and 64,015 yuan/year in urban private units (nominal growth of 3.8%). Non-private urban education averaged 133,539 yuan/year. The statistics cover urban legal entities with 5 or more employees, excluding individually owned businesses and freelancers.

These are industry references only, not occupational percentiles or individual rates.

In mainland China, treatment of cultural relics and collections, conservation materials, and conservator qualification requirements must be verified under the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Protection of Cultural Relics, competent authorities' rules, and institutional procedures. Other jurisdictions' rules cannot substitute.

Museum collection management and treatment documentation requirements follow competent authorities' regulations and institutional rules. Authorization chains for object treatment, loans, and conservation must be confirmed through contracts and policies.

US museum technicians and conservators (O*NET-SOC 25-4013.00) had 2025 median wages of US$24.73/hour and US$51,440/year. The median means half of workers earn above and half below this value. It is not guaranteed entry-level pay, academic pay, or an internal institutional grade.

For the same exact occupation, wages are US$33,780/year at the 10th percentile, US$41,050/year at the 25th, US$67,640/year at the 75th, and US$87,530/year at the 90th. The gap between the extremes generally reflects institution type (museums, government, universities, private organizations), role level, funding cycles, and specialization together. Lower percentiles cannot be labeled starting pay.

Editorial suggestion: Verify role funding sources, contracts, and renewal conditions. BLS notes that federally funded archives and museums are affected by budget changes, but no magnitude of income volatility for this occupation was obtained. Project funding is not wages; wages of paid part-time employees remain within OEWS scope.

When comparing roles, confirm employment type (full-time, part-time, contract, or project-based), contract duration and renewal conditions, travel and courier allowances for collection loans, and whether tools or training costs are personally supplied. These terms can substantially affect actual income.
2025 occupational industry shares: Arts, entertainment, and recreation 45%; government 27%; education 13%; others 15%. These are not industry wages and do not establish reasons for individual pay.

This page does not convert US figures into yuan, replace US occupational wages with Chinese industry averages, or use US wages to estimate Chinese income. The two markets have different statistical definitions and coverage.

entries: O*NET gives this occupation the interest code RC (Realistic, Conventional): a preference for hands-on treatment of physical materials and for recording and acting according to standards and procedures. Interests indicate only willingness to sustain these activities, not ability, hiring, or authorization.
Compare signals with specific conservation tasks, supervisor feedback, and role requirements rather than interest scores alone.
One fit signal is caution and patience: Testing and consulting documentation before treatment, and accepting repeated deliberation and lengthy treatment cycles.
Compare signals with actual condition assessment records, treatment reports, and supervisor feedback.

Another signal is documentation habits: Willingness to photograph, catalog, and preserve treatment records according to standards, clearly explaining the rationale for others to review and monitor later.
Compare signals with collection database entries, treatment reports, and review feedback.

If you dislike prolonged detailed work, document checks, and strict records, compare curatorial work, archives, exhibition design, or archaeology. Institutions differ in the balance of hands-on treatment and research writing.
Compare signals with real role rhythms rather than a single test result.

Do not screen yourself using MBTI, astrology, or one interest score. Start with a paper condition report exercise, then observe your actual response to testing, weighing treatment options, and records.
Use assessments for exploration, not as a basis for hiring or authorization.

Hand steadiness and observation can improve with training. Materials knowledge, testing methods, documentation standards, and ethical principles can also be systematically learned and observed through reports.
Compare capability signals with reviewable treatment records and review comments.

paragraphs: RC interests describe Realistic preferences for handling materials and Conventional preferences for standardized records. They cannot predict hiring, competence, or treatment authorization; extraversion or introversion cannot determine these alone.

Evidence level is exploratory: Interest codes and preparation levels come from the US O*NET occupational profile, without occupation-specific selection validity or adoption evidence. They cannot determine hiring, qualifications, or treatment authorization.

Boundaries: This editorially compiled checklist does not replace conservation ethics, institutional policies, cultural relic protection laws, or professional consultation. Specific treatment authorization, material selection, and documentation requirements follow institutional and competent authority documents.

Key considerations in advance are irreversible treatment and secondary damage, chemical and solvent exposure, dust and mold spores, sharp tools and heavy-object handling, and data and collection information security. Exposure varies across paper, textiles, metals, painted surfaces, and exhibitions.

Evidence scope: Work-context percentages come from the O*NET work-context survey of US respondents and are not extrapolated to other regions. AI and responsibility boundaries reference O*NET tasks and NIST AI RMF 1.0. Chinese wages use and identify the National Bureau of Statistics' 2025 culture, sports, and entertainment industry proxy.
Conservators and technicians performing testing, cleaning, consolidation, infilling, and installation in conservation laboratories, storage rooms, and galleries.

Editorial scenarios include loss of original information, chemical/mold exposure, and missing records. Tasks and ethical guidance do not establish occupational injury, illness, or collection loss rates. Verify specific hazard assessments separately.

Boundaries: The entry route and capability ladder on this page are editorial explanations of control points that can be handled independently, not a uniform ranking or timetable. Specific treatment authorization and qualification requirements follow institutional rules, professional association standards, and competent authorities' rules.
Can move objects, document condition, take photographs, and perform basic cleaning under supervision, completing required record forms.
Assistance and documentation
Can independently assess condition and design tests, propose treatment and no-treatment options, and perform approved low-risk treatments.
Independent assessment and low-risk treatment
Can undertake complete treatment in one material specialty, design and make infills, assess reversibility and long-term stability, and write treatment reports.
Specialized conservation and reporting

Can review others' plans and records, organize interdisciplinary consultation and outside expert handovers, and contribute to preservation environment and risk management policies, without replacing institutional or competent authority responsibilities.

ai_impact_table.responsibility_intro: The steps below describe the sequence of human controls when this occupation uses tools and systems: input verification, conditions of use, output review, and recordkeeping.

responsibility_steps.说明: Check collection files, condition records, treatment history, and research materials, confirming object identity and provenance.
Treat objects only when test data are available, materials and solvents compliant, and protective and workspace conditions met.
Have a person review treatment reversibility and distinguishability, material compatibility, and long-term stability. Do not approve solely on system recommendations.
Record before-and-after photographs, test data, materials and formulations, substances applied and timing, and update collection databases.
Stop and request outside expert consultation when deterioration is uncontrolled, authorization is exceeded, or irreversible treatment is needed.

risks.mitigation: Examine and compare plans first, document within authorization, and assess material stability and future examination and retreatment conditions. AIC infills should be detectable and reversible; this does not require every cleaning/testing action to be fully reversible. Chinese museum relics require graded approvals under Article 62; institutional approval does not replace statutory approval.

risks.title: Irreversible treatment and secondary damage

components.definition_block: The official definition of Museum Technicians and Conservators (O*NET-SOC 25-4013.00) is to restore, maintain, or prepare objects in museum collections for storage, research, or exhibition. They may work with fossils, skeletal parts, or botanical specimens, or with artifacts, textiles, or art; may identify and record objects or install and arrange exhibits; and include book and document conservators.

Internship/volunteer experience helps, and full-time roles require relevant experience. Assistant/training opportunities may be explored as an editorial suggestion, but hiring without conservation experience is not guaranteed.
questions.question: Can I enter without conservation experience?

questions.answer: Extraversion or introversion matters little. The key is endurance for prolonged detailed work and documentation checks and clear communication with curators, collection keepers, architects, and outside experts.
questions.question: Are extraverts or introverts better suited?

questions.answer: New-hire education for this occupation: 73% master's degree, 12% bachelor's degree, 8% postbaccalaureate certificate. JobZone5 is group-level. BLS identifies master's degrees as typical for conservators and bachelor's degrees for technicians. The directory's 621 programs are not uniform education or licensing requirements.
questions.question: What education, training, and qualifications are typically needed to enter?

questions.answer: No. Assessment results support self-exploration only and do not constitute evidence for hiring, qualifications, or physical treatment authorization.
questions.question: Can assessment results serve as evidence for hiring or treatment authorization?

questions.answer: O*NET currently found no certifications, which does not establish that the field has none or that qualifications are unnecessary in China. Verify education, individual technical titles, organizational conservation qualifications, and approvals for specific objects separately.
questions.question: Is professional certification required?

questions.answer: The impact is substantial: O*NET work context shows 76% use their hands to handle or feel objects almost continually and 96% consider accuracy extremely important. Contaminant and chemical contact requires protection according to procedures.
questions.question: Do prolonged fine work and chemical contact significantly affect fit?

questions.answer: Retain condition assessment forms, test data, plans and approval records, before-and-after photographs, material and formulation records, and records confirming database entry and object number consistency.
questions.question: How can I build reviewable professional evidence?

questions.answer: Start with a paper condition report exercise: Use a fictional object file to describe tests, treatment comparisons, risk and reversibility assessments, and record fields, then review against public professional guidance.
questions.question: What low-cost trial should I start with?

signals.body: Testing and consulting documentation before treatment, accepting repeated deliberation and lengthy cycles, and photographing, cataloging, and retaining treatment records according to standards.
signals.label: Fit signals

signals.body: A tendency to treat without testing, obscure original information with irreversible materials, or proceed with high-risk treatments despite incomplete records.
signals.label: Signals requiring caution

signals.body: Use an entirely fictional object file for a paper condition report: Describe tests, treatment and no-treatment options, risk and reversibility assessments, approval and record fields, and three safety and ethical confirmation points.

description.text: Museum technicians and conservators (O*NET-SOC 25-4013.00) prepare museum objects for preservation, research, and exhibition: assess conservation needs, select safe and effective methods, clean and consolidate objects, document condition and treatment plans, install and arrange exhibitions, and maintain collection databases. This page compiles official O*NET tasks and work context, Job Zone 5 and graduate education routes, the US 2025 BLS OEWS median annual wage of US$51,440 and 5% employment growth for 2024—2034 (Bright Outlook), mainland Chinese culture, sports, and entertainment industry proxy wages, AI and responsibility boundaries, fit signals, and entry routes.

subject.name: Museum Technicians and Conservators
subject.summary: Museum technicians and conservators (O*NET-SOC 25-4013.00) prepare and conserve museum objects for preservation, research, and exhibition: determine whether objects need conservation and select the safest and most effective methods; clean and consolidate materials such as paper, textiles, wood, metal, glass, ceramics, and furniture; document condition, treatment plans, and methods; install and arrange objects for exhibitions; and maintain collection databases. This page uses official sources only to explain occupational scope, tasks, preparation requirements, and statistical definitions.
